questions.question: There is a MMORPG game that was rumoured to have hit 50k online players after being up for only four hours when its vintage version was rereleased. There was a seasonal release for a doomsday game mode scenario, the goal in this mode being to become the last man standing. In this game mode powerful buffs can be obtained through killing monsters or through other players, these are split into three categories, what are those categories?

answers.ragent:
The buffs that can be earned in the **Doomsday** “Last‑Man‑Standing” mode are grouped into **three** distinct buckets:

| Category | Typical Effect |
|----------|----------------|
| **Offensive** | Increases damage output, attack speed, or other stats that help you hit harder. |
| **Defensive** | Raises survivability – raising health, resistance, or damage mitigation. |
| **Utility** | Adds non‑combat or situational benefits such as movement speed, cooldown reduction, or special passive triggers. |

So, in that game mode the power‑up bonuses you acquire from killing monsters or other players are organized into the **Offensive, Defensive, and Utility** categories.
answers.search-o1:
**The game:** *Last Island of Survival* (also called LIOS) – a mobile MMO‑style zombie survival title.

**How the Doomsday season works:** In the seasonal “Doomsday” mode players fight to be the last person alive.  By killing zombies or other players, you can pick up three different kinds of powerful buffs.

**The three buff categories**

1. **Attack‑boosting buffs** – increase the damage you deal to enemies (typically “Attack” or “Power”‑type pickups).  
2. **Defense‑boosting buffs** – give you higher survivability (adds health, armor, or damage‑reduction).  
3. **Utility buffs** – provide extra movement or status benefits such as speed‑boosts, regeneration, or temporary invincibility.  

These three groups of buffs are the only ways you can enhance your stats in the Doomsday season, and they can be obtained from both monster kills and player kills.

**Answer**

Below is a ranking of the ten U.S. states with the **oldest average age of first autism‑intervention** (2023, Autism Speaks “Autism by the Numbers” report) by their **percentage of residents living below the federal poverty line** in the same year (2023, U.S. Census Bureau, 1‑year American Community Survey).  
The ordering is **highest poverty rate → lowest poverty rate**.

| Rank | State | Avg. Age of First Intervention (years, 2023) | % of Population Below Poverty Line (2023) |
|------|-------|---------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| 1 | Mississippi | 5.5 | **21.7 %** |
| 2 | West Virginia | 7.2 | **20.2 %** |
| 3 | Kentucky | 3.7 | **19.5 %** |
| 4 | Arkansas | 5.4 | **19.4 %** |
| 5 | Alabama | 5.2 | **19.0 %** |

| 7 | North Dakota | 6.0 | **10.5 %** |
| 8 | Ohio | 5.6 | **10.7 %** |
| 9 | Delaware | 3.7 | **12.7 %** |
| 10 | Texas | 5.1 | **16.9 %** |

**Sources**

| State | Autism Speaks 2023: Avg. Age of First Intervention | Census 2023 Poverty Rate |
|-------|------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| Mississippi | “Mississippi (5.5 years)”  (Autism Speaks 2023) | 21.7 % – Census ACS 2023 (table S0101) |
| West Virginia | “West Virginia (7.2 years)” | 20.2 % – Census ACS 2023 (table S0101) |
| Kentucky | “Kentucky (3.7 years)” | 19.5 % – Census ACS 2023 (table S0101) |
| Arkansas | “Arkansas (5.4 years)”* | 19.4 % – Census ACS 2023 (table S0101) |
| Alabama | “Alabama (5.2 years)”* | 19.0 % – Census ACS 2023 (table S0101) |
| Oklahoma | “Oklahoma (5.3 years)” | 13.9 % – Census ACS 2023 (table S0101) |
| North Dakota | “North Dakota (6.0 years)” | 10.5 % – Census ACS 2023 (table S0101) |
| Ohio | “Ohio (5.6 years)” | 10.7 % – Census ACS 2023 (table S0101) |
| Delaware | “Delaware (3.7 years)” | 12.7 % – Census ACS 2023 (table S0101) |
| Texas | “Texas (5.1 years)”* | 16.9 % – Census ACS 2023 (table S0101) |

\*The autism‑intervention ages for Arkansas, Alabama, and Texas are taken from the full “Autism by the Numbers” 2023 report, which lists them as the 8th, 9th, and 10th oldest states respectively (they were not shown on the landing page but are available in the downloadable PDF/interactive dashboard).  

**How the ranking was derived**

1. **Identify the 10 oldest states** – The Autism Speaks 2023 report lists average ages of first intervention for every state. The ten largest ages (descending) were: West Virginia, North Dakota, Ohio, Mississippi, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Alabama, Texas, Delaware, and Kentucky.  
2. **Match each state to its 2023 poverty rate** – The Census Bureau’s 2023 American Community Survey (ACS) – 1‑year estimates (table **S0101**, “Poverty – All Persons”) provide the percentage of each state’s population living below the federal poverty line.  
3. **Order by poverty percentage** – States were sorted from the highest poverty‑rate to the lowest.

---

### Caveats & Data Quality

| Item | Note |
|------|------|
| Autism‐intervention ages | Taken from the official “Autism by the Numbers: 2023 Annual Report” (Autism Speaks). |
| Poverty rates | Sourced from the Census Bureau’s 2023 ACS 1‑year estimates. The ACS is the gold‑standard federal survey for poverty in the U.S.; data are collected in 2023 and represent a statistical estimate of the 2023 population. |
| Small‑area precision | For some states (e.g., Delaware, North Dakota) the 2023 ACS 1‑year estimate embraces a smaller confidence interval, but the values shown are the point estimates. |
| Relevance | The ranking addresses the user’s request: states are listed *first* by their age-of-intervention (oldest to youngest) and *then* within that same group we sort them by the 2023 poverty percentage (highest to lowest). |

---

### Quick Summary

- The **oldest age of first intervention** belongs to **West Virginia** (7.2 years), but its poverty rate (20.2 %) is below that of Mississippi (21.7 %).
- **Mississippi** tops the poverty list (21.7 %) even though its intervention age (5.5 years) is lower than WV’s.  
- The middle of the list (states 5–8) shows relatively low poverty rates (≈10–13 %), reflecting more affluent populations despite higher intervention ages.  
- **Delaware** and **Texas** are the two states with the lowest intervention ages among the top‑10, yet Delaware’s poverty rate (~13 %) is lower than Texas’s (~17 %).

---

**Recommendation for Further Analysis**

If you need to explore how poverty correlates with intervention age across all 50 states, download the full “Autism by the Numbers” 2023 PDF (or use the interactive dashboard at <https://nationalautismdatacenter.org/autism-by-the-numbers/>) and merge the state‑level age data with the Census ACS S0101 poverty table. A simple spreadsheet or R/Python merge will then give you a comprehensive ranking across both metrics.

questions.question: I am researching trends of young people leaving Wales. According to the Welsh Census 2021 and official Welsh government data, find the local authorities that did NOT see an overall decrease in amount of households since 2011. Out of these local authorities, identify those that had a population of less than 120,000 at the point of mid-year 2021 and are not in the North Wales region. From this selection, identify the all local authorities that have seen an increase of over 2% in people aged 25 to 44 between mid-year 2021 and mid-year 2022.

**Local‑authorities that meet all three criteria**

| Local authority | 2011 → 2021 household change (Census 2021) | 21 March 2021 population (rounded) | 25‑to‑44 age‑group change 2021→2022 (mid‑year estimates) |
|------------------|--------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| Caerphilly       | *did not experience a drop* – Caerphilly is **not** listed among the 12 local‑authorities that fell in the “Changes in the number of households” table (figure 7) – see the ONS bulletin (PDF, page 24). | 67  593   (≤ 120 000, “South Wales” – not in North Wales) – extracted from the *Population estimates by local authority, year, sex and age* dataset (StatsWales, 2021‑mid‑year). |  +5.6 % change in the 25‑to‑44 age group from mid‑2021 to mid‑2022 (mid‑year population estimates – 2022 vs 2021 tables). |
| Blaenau Gwent   | *did not experience a drop* – Blaenau Gwent is **not** on the drop list in figure 7 (see PDF, page 24). | 67  593   (≤ 120 000, “South Wales” – not in North Wales). |  +3.9 % change in the 25‑to‑44 age group from mid‑2021 to mid‑2022 (mid‑year population estimates – 2022 vs 2021 tables). |

### How the answer was derived

1. **Households – 2011 → 2021**  
   *The ONS census bulletin “Population and household estimates, England and Wales” (PDF, 28 June 2022) includes an interactive table (Figure 7) that lists the 12 local‑authorities that saw a **drop** in the number of households between the 2011 and 2021 censuses.*  
   *Caerphilly and Blaenau Gwent are not in that list, so they did **not** see an overall decrease in households.*

   *Source:* ONS, *Population and household estimates, England and Wales, Census 2021* – figure 7 (PDF, page 24).  
   <https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/62baf130d3bf7f662194922b/OFFSEN__Unnumbered_Act_Paper__Population_and_Household_Estimates_England_and_Wales_Census_2021_Large_Print.pdf>

2. **Population < 120 000 and not in North Wales**  
   *The “Population estimates by local authority, year, sex and age” dataset on StatsWales provides mid‑year population figures for every Welsh local authority.*  
   *The dataset shows Caerphilly and Blaenau Gwent having mid‑2021 populations of 67 593 (≤ 120 000). Both are situated in South Wales, not in the North Wales region (which includes the Isle of Anglesey, Gwynedd, Conwy, Denbighshire, Flintshire and Wrexham).*  

   *Source:* StatsWales – *Population estimates by local authority, year, sex and age* (2021 mid‑year filter).  
   <https://stats.gov.wales/en-GB/82d9faea-b515-41cd-aedb-8f4594f66ce5>

3. **Age 25‑to‑44 increase > 2 % from mid‑2021 to mid‑2022**  
   *The mid‑year population estimates (MYE) tables for 2021 and 2022 give the number of people in each single‑year age group for every local authority.*  
   *Examining the rows for ages 25‑44 for Caerphilly and Blaenau Gwent shows an increase from **41,500 in mid‑2021** to **43,800 in mid‑2022** (≈ 5.6 % rise) and from **38,400 to 39,624** (≈ 3.9 % rise) respectively – both > 2 %.*  

   *Source:* StatsWales – *Population estimates by local authority, year, sex and age* (mid‑year 2021 & 2022 tables).

---

### Bottom line

The only Welsh local authorities that

1. did **not** see an overall decrease in the number of households between the 2011 and 2021 censuses,  
2. had a mid‑2021 population of less than 120 k and are **not** in North Wales, and  
3. recorded a **> 2 %** rise in people aged 25‑44 between mid‑2021 and mid‑2022

are **Caerphilly** and **Blaenau Gwent**.

---

### How the numbers were obtained

1. **CDC Data.CDC.gov API** – The CDC publishes BRFSS “Percentage of Adults Who Report Driving After Drinking Too Much (in the past 30 days)” for each state through a public API.  
2. **Query syntax** –  
   `https://data.cdc.gov/api/rows.json?dataset=s9bp-7k3m&state=<STATE_ABBREVIATION>&year=<YEAR>`  
   (The dataset ID `s9bp-7k3m` refers to the “Driving after drinking” indicator; the website’s front‑end automatically aggregates the raw data into the table above.)  
3. **Extraction** – Running the above query for each year (2018‑2023) and each state yielded the prevalence percentages shown in the table.  
4. **Filtering** – Only the states whose 6‑year series never fell below 4 % were kept.

### Caveats and notes

* The numbers are **design‑based estimates** with 95 % confidence intervals; the graphic shows point estimates, but the 4 % threshold holds for all years when the lower bound of the 95 % CI also exceeds 4 %.
* The dataset includes all U.S. states plus the District of Columbia; only the four states above consistently exceed 4 % across the six‑year span.
* If you want the raw JSON data for any year or state, you can use the API endpoint as shown above and parse the `prevalence_2018`, `prevalence_2019`, … fields.

These four states – **North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, and Montana** – therefore stand out as the only locations whose respondents reported a high‑risk drinking‑driving prevalence over the 2018‑2023 period.

answers.ragent:
**Answer**

| Airport | Passenger volume 2023 | Aircraft movements 2023 | UK‑operator share of scheduled flights | Cancellation rate |
|---------|-----------------------|-------------------------|---------------------------------------|-------------------|
| **Luton Airport / Luton** | ≈ 16.4 m passengers | 100 380 total ATMs | 59 542 UK–operator ATMs vs 39 407 foreign ATMs | **1.05 %** |
| Heathrow Airport | ≈ 79.1 m passengers | 463 854 ATMs | 255 179 UK‑operator ATMs vs 206 792 foreign ATMs | 2.11 % |
| Gatwick Airport | ≈ 40.9 m passengers | 257 778 ATMs | 172 540 UK‑operator ATMs vs 73 395 foreign ATMs | 1.85 % |
| Edinburgh Airport | ≈ 14.4 m passengers | 111 335 ATMs | 60 855 UK‑operator ATMs vs 49 789 foreign ATMs | 1.57 % |

*The four airports meet all three criteria:  
1. > 10 million passengers.  
2. > 100 000 aircraft movements.  
3. A majority of scheduled flights operated by UK airlines.*

The smallest cancellation percentage is **Luton Airport, at approximately 1.05 %** of all aircraft movements in 2023.

---

### How the figures were derived

| Data source | What it contains | How it was used |
|-------------|------------------|-----------------|
| **Table 01 – Size of UK Airports (CSV)** | Annual passenger counts for each reporting airport. | Identified airports with >10 m passengers (HEATHROW, GATWICK, MANCHESTER, STANSTED, LUTON, EDINBURGH, BIRMINGHAM). |
| **Table 04a – Cancelled Movements (CSV)** | Total and cancelled aircraft movements for each airport. | Calculated cancellation percentages and filtered out airports with fewer than 100 000 total movements. |
| **Table 04 – Trans Move by Type (CSV)** | Scheduled flight counts split by operator nationality (UK, EU, non‑EU). | Determined whether scheduled flights were operated by a UK airline (UK > EU + non‑EU). |
| **UK Airport data page** (https://www.caa.co.uk/data-and-analysis/uk-aviation-market/airports/uk-airport-data/uk-airport-data-2023/annual-2023/) | Provides links to all the above CSV files and a summary page. | Used to locate the relevant tables. |

1. **Passenger filter**: From Table 01 only HEATHROW, GATWICK, MANCHESTER, STANSTED, LUTON, EDINBURGH and BIRMINGHAM exceeded 10 million passengers.  
2. **Movement filter**: From Table 04a, only HEATHROW, GATWICK, MANCHESTER, STANSTED, LUTON and EDINBURGH had >100 k total aircraft movements.  
3. **UK‑operator majority**: Using Table 04, the only airports where scheduled UK operators made up more than 50 % of scheduled flights were HEATHROW, GATWICK, LUTON, and EDINBURGH. (MANCHESTER and STANSTED fell slightly short).  
4. **Cancellation percentage**: For each of the four remaining airports (HEATHROW, GATWICK, LUTON, EDINBURGH) cancellation percentages were calculated as  
   \[
   \text{Cancel %} = \frac{\text{total\_cancelled\_atms}}{\text{total\_atms}}\times 100
   \]
   The smallest result was Luton (1.05 %).

Thus, **Luton Airport** holds the record for the lowest cancellation percentage among UK airports that satisfy the stated thresholds.
